Compliance requirements dictate that all table data must be encrypted at rest using a dedicated encryption key managed by the organization in AWS KMS, with the ability to audit key usage. How should the Solutions Architect configure DynamoDB encryption?

options.text: Write custom application code to encrypt every table attribute locally using AES-256 before writing items to DynamoDB.
Enable server-side encryption on the DynamoDB table using an AWS KMS customer managed key (CMK).
Attach an IAM permissions boundary to the DynamoDB table to enforce encryption standards at runtime.
Rely on DynamoDB default encryption, which uses AWS-owned keys automatically without customer configuration.

questions.explanation: Amazon DynamoDB encryption at rest supports customer managed keys (CMKs) in AWS KMS. This integration fulfills compliance standards for dedicated key management and full auditability via AWS CloudTrail.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Client-side encryption introduces complex key management overhead and prevents native DynamoDB operations like querying or indexing encrypted attributes directly.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Permissions boundaries restrict IAM principals, not the storage engine encryption mechanisms of database tables.
wrongOptionNotes.D: AWS-owned keys do not provide customer auditing control or custom key management required by strict financial compliance mandates.

questions.question: An enterprise web application runs on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets. The instances frequently need to download software patches and updates from external public repositories. Security guidelines mandate that all outbound internet traffic from private instances must be inspected and filtered by fully qualified domain name (FQDN). Which AWS service should the Solutions Architect use?

options.text: AWS WAF
AWS Network Firewall
Standard NAT Gateways
Amazon VPC Security Groups

questions.explanation: AWS Network Firewall allows security teams to create custom firewall rules with stateful domain name filtering (FQDN), enabling precise control over outbound traffic from private VPC subnets to external repositories.

wrongOptionNotes.A: AWS WAF protects HTTP/HTTPS web applications against web exploits at the application layer, but does not inspect general TCP/UDP outbound traffic from private EC2 subnets.
wrongOptionNotes.C: NAT Gateways provide IP translation for internet access, but do not offer application-layer FQDN inspection or URL filtering.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Security groups operate at the IP address and port level; they cannot filter outbound traffic based on domain names (FQDNs).

questions.question: An e-commerce platform runs its primary transactional database on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. The application experiences predictable traffic spikes during evening hours, but remains mostly idle overnight. Management requires a significant cost reduction for the database tier without risking performance bottlenecks during peak hours.

options.text: Use AWS Lambda to stop the RDS instance every night and start it every morning.
Migrate the database to Amazon Aurora Serverless v2, configuring minimum and maximum ACUs to match the workload patterns.
Purchase 3-year All Upfront Reserved Instances for the current RDS PostgreSQL instance size.
Scale down the RDS instance manually twice a day using AWS Systems Manager automation documents.

questions.explanation: Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 provides fine-grained, second-by-second capacity scaling, matching resource allocation directly to demand and making it ideal for workloads with predictable spikes and long idle periods.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Stopping a production database for several hours each night would cause severe application downtime, rendering the system unavailable for overnight batch jobs or global users.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While RIs offer discounts for steady workloads, they do not optimize costs for idle overnight periods since you pay for the provisioned capacity 24/7 regardless of actual usage.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Manual or automated vertical scaling of RDS instances involves rebooting the database engine, causing unnecessary downtime and failing to provide instantaneous scaling for sudden traffic spikes.

questions.question: A global gaming company hosts a multiplayer backend on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The traffic fluctuates heavily based on time zones, but the baseline baseline capacity remains steady. Finance wants to minimize the compute bill while maintaining high availability across multiple Availability Zones.

options.text: Migrate the entire workload to AWS Lambda without reviewing execution duration or payload sizes.
Purchase Compute Savings Plans covering the baseline usage and use an Auto Scaling group with Spot Instances for the variable spikes.
Purchase Standard Reserved Instances for the maximum possible peak load expected during the year.
Deploy all instances as Amazon EC2 Spot Instances in a single Availability Zone to maximize cost savings.

questions.explanation: Combining Compute Savings Plans for predictable baseline capacity with an Auto Scaling group utilizing Spot Instances for dynamic spikes optimizes both compute costs and fault tolerance.

wrongOptionNotes.A: For continuous, long-running multiplayer backend servers, AWS Lambda can be significantly more expensive and architecturally unsuitable compared to running on EC2.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Purchasing RIs for peak capacity results in wasted spend during off-peak hours when those instances sit idle or underutilized.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Using a single Availability Zone violates high availability requirements, and relying entirely on Spot Instances for baseline production workloads risks sudden termination without fallback capacity.

questions.question: An enterprise analytics team processes hundreds of gigabytes of clickstream data daily using an Apache Spark application. The job runs inside an Amazon ECS cluster running on Amazon EC2 worker nodes. The jobs are scheduled to run only twice a day, but the EC2 instances remain provisioned 24/7.

options.text: Configure an AWS Auto Scaling lifecycle hook to terminate the EC2 instances when idle.
Purchase 1-year Standard Reserved Instances for the ECS container instances.
Re-architect the ECS tasks to run on AWS Fargate, and trigger them using EventBridge schedules.
Migrate the Spark job to Amazon EMR and use long-running core nodes with transient task nodes.

questions.explanation: For intermittent workloads running on containers, moving from EC2-backed ECS to AWS Fargate eliminates idle instance costs by billing strictly for active execution time.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Lifecycle hooks manage state transitions during termination or startup, but they do not provide a native scheduling mechanism to turn cluster instances off and on based on a daily timetable.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Purchasing RIs for instances that run only twice a day still leaves them provisioned and billed 24/7, failing to address the fundamental inefficiency of keeping idle hardware running.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Maintaining core nodes long-running on EMR still incurs continuous infrastructure costs, whereas serverless containers (Fargate) or transient EMR clusters would be more cost-effective.

questions.question: A financial data provider stores 100 TB of historical audit logs in Amazon S3 Standard. Regulations require these logs to be retained for 7 years. Once written, the logs are almost never read unless an external audit is triggered, which happens approximately once every two years.

options.text: Transition the logs to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) using an S3 Lifecycle policy.
Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering to automatically move objects between frequent and infrequent access tiers.
Compress the logs into a single large tarball and store them on Amazon EBS volumes attached to an idle EC2 instance.
Implement an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects immediately to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

questions.explanation: S3 Glacier Deep Archive provides the absolute lowest-cost long-term archival storage for data accessed rarely or never, perfectly aligning with multi-year compliance retention requirements.

wrongOptionNotes.A: S3 Standard-IA is designed for data accessed more frequently than once a month and carries higher per-gigabyte storage costs compared to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
wrongOptionNotes.B: S3 Intelligent-Tiering has a small monthly monitoring and automation fee per object, which is unnecessary for data that is definitively known to be accessed less than once a year.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Storing backup data on EBS volumes attached to EC2 is extremely costly, lacks native durability guarantees of S3, and introduces single points of failure.

questions.question: A software company operates a microservices architecture on Amazon EKS. Developers frequently deploy non-production preview environments that stay active indefinitely because teams forget to clean them up, causing unexpected cloud billing spikes at the end of every month.

options.text: Implement AWS Budgets actions to automatically terminate non-production EKS namespaces and scale down worker nodes when budget thresholds are exceeded.
Migrate the development EKS cluster to AWS Outposts to reduce data transfer fees.
Deploy AWS Trusted Advisor checks and rely on manual email notifications sent to project managers.
Purchase Amazon EC2 Instance Savings Plans for the non-production development cluster.

questions.explanation: AWS Budgets supports automated actions that can execute remediation workflows when spending targets are breached, helping control rogue or forgotten non-production resources.

wrongOptionNotes.B: AWS Outposts is an on-premises infrastructure service that involves high upfront costs and does not solve the issue of unmanaged, forgotten development environments.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Relying on manual email notifications does not prevent forgotten resources from running continuously; proactive automated remediation is required.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Savings Plans lock you into a commitment for 1 or 3 years, which is counterproductive for transient or poorly managed temporary workloads.

questions.question: A digital marketing agency maintains a high-traffic asset delivery platform fronted by Amazon CloudFront. The origin server is an Amazon S3 bucket containing high-resolution images and videos. The finance department notes that data egress charges from CloudFront to the internet are exceptionally high.

options.text: Enable CloudFront Origin Shield and configure aggressive caching behaviors with optimized TTLs on CloudFront distributions.
Move the S3 bucket to a different AWS Region closer to the primary development team.
Replace CloudFront with an Application LoadBalancer directly in front of the S3 bucket to serve assets.
Enable Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) on the S3 bucket.

questions.explanation: Maximizing cache hit ratios through proper TTL tuning and implementing CloudFront Origin Shield minimizes requests hitting the origin, significantly reducing overall data transfer and storage retrieval costs.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Moving the S3 bucket does not reduce end-user data egress costs, as global viewers will still incur standard CloudFront-to-internet data transfer rates.
wrongOptionNotes.C: An ALB cannot cache content effectively like a CDN, and routing all global traffic directly through an ALB increases data transfer and infrastructure costs.
wrongOptionNotes.D: CORS is a security mechanism that controls browser access to resources from different domains; it has no impact on data transfer costs or caching efficiency.

questions.question: An enterprise organization has 50 distinct AWS accounts managed under AWS Organizations. The central cloud financial management team needs granular visibility into cost drivers, cross-account data transfer fees, and daily spending anomalies across all business units.

options.text: Deploy a custom AWS Lambda function in the master account that calls DescribeInstances on all member accounts every hour.
Purchase All Upfront Reserved Instances across all accounts to prevent budget overruns.
Enable AWS Cost Anomaly Detection, set up AWS Cost Categories, and activate AWS Cost Explorer with daily granularity and hourly data export to Amazon S3.
Log into each individual AWS account's billing console on the first of every month and export CSV reports manually.

questions.explanation: AWS Cost Explorer, Cost Categories, and Cost Anomaly Detection provide enterprise-grade visibility, categorization, and alerting for multi-account AWS environments.

wrongOptionNotes.A: API polling for infrastructure metadata does not provide financial billing metrics, cost allocation data, or usage anomaly tracking.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Purchasing RIs provides billing discounts but does not offer cost visibility, reporting granularity, or anomaly detection capabilities.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Manual reporting across 50 accounts is unscalable, error-prone, and lacks real-time anomaly detection.

questions.question: A financial analytics firm runs a batch data processing pipeline using Amazon EC2 instances. The jobs take between 30 minutes and 2 hours to complete and can be safely interrupted and resumed if necessary. The company wants to minimize the compute costs for these batch workloads.

options.text: Use Amazon RDS read replicas to execute the batch processing scripts inside PostgreSQL stored procedures.
Use AWS Batch configured with Amazon EC2 Spot Instances across multiple instance types and Availability Zones.
Provision a fixed fleet of Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances with 3-year Compute Savings Plans.
Deploy the processing jobs as long-running AWS Lambda functions with maximum timeout limits configured.

questions.explanation: AWS Batch combined with EC2 Spot Instances is the optimal architectural pattern for fault-tolerant, interruptible batch processing jobs at the lowest possible cost.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Executing heavy analytical batch processing inside a relational database engine is an architectural anti-pattern that degrades database performance and spikes compute costs.
wrongOptionNotes.C: On-Demand instances, even with Savings Plans, are significantly more expensive than Spot Instances for interruptible batch workloads.
wrongOptionNotes.D: AWS Lambda has a strict maximum execution limit of 15 minutes, making it unsuitable for batch jobs that take up to 2 hours.

questions.question: A healthcare startup stores medical imaging datasets in Amazon S3. Regulations mandate that data must be retained for 5 years. Access frequency is high during the first 30 days after upload, moderate between 31 and 90 days, and extremely rare after 90 days.

options.text: Configure an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days, and to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 90 days.
Leave all imaging datasets in S3 Standard and purchase S3 Reserved Storage capacity.
Use Amazon EBS gp3 volumes attached to an EC2 instance to store all 5 years of imaging data.
Move all files immediately to S3 Glacier Deep Archive upon upload to maximize savings.

questions.explanation: S3 Lifecycle policies enable automated, cost-effective tiering of data across storage classes based on access patterns over time.

wrongOptionNotes.B: S3 does not offer reserved storage capacity models; data is billed based on tiered storage classes and actual gigabytes used.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Storing multi-terabyte datasets on EBS is cost-prohibitive and lacks the native multi-AZ durability and lifecycle automation of Amazon S3.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Immediate transition to Glacier Deep Archive would impair daily operations because the medical imaging data is accessed frequently during the first 30 days.

questions.question: An enterprise web application runs on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The application connects to an Amazon RDS for MySQL database. During traffic surges, application servers scale out correctly, but the database experiences high CPU utilization due to repetitive read queries, causing latency spikes.

options.text: Deploy Amazon ElastiCache for Redis in front of the database to cache frequent query results and reduce database read load.
Migrate the database to Amazon Redshift for transactional processing.
Upgrade the primary RDS database instance class to a significantly larger memory-optimized instance.
Increase the maximum size of the EC2 Auto Scaling group to handle more application requests.

questions.explanation: Implementing an in-memory caching layer using Amazon ElastiCache reduces direct database read queries, optimizing performance and avoiding costly vertical database upgrades.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Amazon Redshift is an OLAP data warehouse and is fundamentally unsuited for transactional (OLTP) application workloads.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Vertical scaling is expensive and only temporarily masks architectural inefficiencies. Caching frequent reads is a more cost-optimized solution.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Adding more application servers will only send more concurrent queries to the database, exacerbating the database CPU bottleneck.

questions.question: A media streaming company operates an application that generates significant outbound data transfer charges because users download large video clips directly from Amazon EC2 instances across multiple AWS regions.

options.text: Configure VPC peering between all AWS regions to streamline video delivery.
Front the EC2 instances with Amazon CloudFront and store the video files in an Amazon S3 bucket instead of local EC2 storage.
Purchase AWS Direct Connect connections in every region where customers reside.
Migrate all EC2 instances to AWS Lambda functions running in the edge locations.

questions.explanation: Using Amazon S3 as the content repository fronted by Amazon CloudFront minimizes expensive EC2 bandwidth costs and takes advantage of edge caching.

wrongOptionNotes.A: VPC peering cannot span across different AWS regions (inter-region VPC peering incurs standard cross-region data transfer fees).
wrongOptionNotes.C: Direct Connect is designed for dedicated private connections between on-premises datacenters and AWS, not for serving public end-users globally.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Lambda@Edge is designed for lightweight request manipulation, not for storing and streaming large video files.

questions.question: An analytics startup runs a data warehouse on Amazon Redshift consisting of 4 dc2.large nodes. The query volume is low during business hours and almost zero overnight. The finance team wants to reduce the Redshift cluster operational costs.

options.text: Delete the Redshift cluster every evening and restore it from an automated snapshot every morning.
Pause and resume the Redshift cluster using AWS Lambda and Amazon EventBridge schedules when queries are not being executed.
Convert the cluster to use single-node RA3 instances without backups.
Migrate all Redshift tables to Amazon DynamoDB.

questions.explanation: Pausing Amazon Redshift clusters during idle periods is a native cost-optimization feature that stops compute charges without data loss.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Restoring a Redshift cluster from a snapshot takes considerable time and incurs snapshot restoration overhead, making daily delete/restore impractical.
wrongOptionNotes.C: RA3 instances are designed for large-scale datasets (managed storage), and disabling backups violates data durability best practices.
wrongOptionNotes.D: DynamoDB is a NoSQL key-value database unsuited for complex analytical SQL queries traditionally run on Redshift.

questions.question: A financial enterprise runs a mission-critical relational database on Amazon RDS for Oracle. The license costs associated with the commercial database engine are extremely high, and management wants to migrate the workload to an open-source engine on AWS to reduce ongoing software licensing expenses.

options.text: Use the AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) and AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) to migrate the schema and data to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL.
Migrate the Oracle database tables into flat CSV files stored in Amazon S3 and query them using Amazon Athena.
Move the database to Amazon DynamoDB without modifying the application SQL queries.
Deploy Oracle Database on Amazon EC2 using Bring Your Own License (BYOL) models.

questions.explanation: Migrating commercial database engines like Oracle to open-source or fully managed engines like Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL eliminates costly commercial software licenses.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Athena is for analytical queries on object storage and cannot support low-latency transactional (OLTP) workloads.
wrongOptionNotes.C: DynamoDB uses a NoSQL API and cannot execute SQL queries, which would require a complete rewrite of the application database layer.
wrongOptionNotes.D: BYOL still requires purchasing and maintaining expensive commercial Oracle licenses, failing to achieve the goal of reducing software licensing costs.

questions.question: A multinational corporation has hundreds of AWS accounts distributed across multiple business units. The central cloud team identifies that millions of dollars are being wasted on unattached Amazon EBS volumes and old RDS database snapshots left behind by terminated projects.

options.text: Purchase All Upfront Savings Plans for all EBS storage volumes across the enterprise.
Enable AWS CloudTrail log analysis in Amazon Athena to manually inspect every API call made in the past year.
Write a bash script to iterate through every region in the master account and delete all EBS volumes.
Deploy AWS Trusted Advisor cross-account aggregation or AWS Compute Optimizer to identify idle resources, and use AWS Systems Manager Automation to clean up unattached EBS volumes.

questions.explanation: Using AWS Trusted Advisor and Compute Optimizer in conjunction with AWS Systems Manager Automation provides an enterprise-scale mechanism to detect and remediate infrastructure waste.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Purchasing savings plans or commitments for unattached, idle resources locks in wasted spend rather than eliminating the waste.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Analyzing CloudTrail logs is an inefficient way to discover currently unattached EBS volumes compared to native cost optimization tools.
wrongOptionNotes.C: A script in the master account cannot directly access or delete resources in separate member AWS accounts without proper cross-account IAM configuration.

questions.question: An online ticketing platform experiences massive, unpredictable traffic spikes during major event ticket releases. The application architecture runs on Amazon EC2 instances inside an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. During these events, scaling out takes too long because application servers require 5 minutes to bootstrap and load dependencies upon startup.

options.text: Configure the Auto Scaling group to use Spot Instances exclusively with a target tracking scaling policy.
Create a golden AMI containing pre-installed application code and dependencies, and use EC2 Auto Scaling warm pools.
Provision a massive fleet of permanent On-Demand EC2 instances to cover the maximum possible peak load.
Migrate the application to Amazon RDS stored procedures to handle client requests instantly.

questions.explanation: Pre-baked golden AMIs combined with Auto Scaling warm pools ensure rapid response times to sudden traffic spikes while avoiding permanent over-provisioning.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Spot Instances can be interrupted with a 2-minute warning, which is dangerous for high-demand ticket sales events where stability is paramount.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Provisioning peak capacity permanently results in extreme over-provisioning and excessive infrastructure costs during normal operational hours.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Relational database stored procedures cannot host front-end web application logic or handle HTTP web traffic.

questions.question: A global SaaS provider runs its primary transactional workload in the us-east-1 Region and requires a disaster recovery (DR) solution in us-west-2. The Recovery Point Objective (RPO) must be under 1 second, and the Recovery Time Objective (RTO) must be under 30 seconds. The workload uses Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. Which architecture meets these requirements with the lowest cost and operational complexity?

options.text: Set up cross-region asynchronous snapshot copy from us-east-1 to us-west-2 every 15 minutes, restoring snapshots to a standby RDS instance during an outage.

Deploy an Amazon Aurora Global Database with a secondary read replica in us-west-2. Configure Amazon Route 53 health checks to trigger a Lambda function that promotes the secondary region database to primary upon primary failure.
Configure an Amazon Aurora Global Database with a secondary read-write capable instance in us-west-2, using automated failover policies.
Deploy an independent Aurora PostgreSQL cluster in us-west-2 and use AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) continuous replication to keep it synchronized.

questions.explanation: Amazon Aurora Global Databases replicate data across AWS Regions with a typical latency of less than a second, satisfying strict RPO requirements. To achieve a fast RTO under 30 seconds for disaster recovery, an automated orchestration mechanism using Route 53 health checks and a Lambda function to promote the secondary DB cluster is necessary since Aurora Global Database cross-region failover requires promotion of the secondary region.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Snapshot copy intervals of 15 minutes result in an RPO of 15 minutes, which completely violates the sub-second RPO requirement.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Amazon Aurora Global Databases support cross-region physical replication with RPO under 1 second, but automated failover to a promoted primary writer in the secondary region is not supported; failover must be manually promoted or orchestrated via application logic, failing the 30-second RTO requirement without custom orchestration scripts, and secondary regions only support read operations until promoted.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While DMS continuous replication can achieve low lag, managing DMS tasks across regions introduces additional operational overhead and failure points compared to Aurora Global Databases native replication.

questions.question: An enterprise web application runs in the us-east-1 Region behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) backed by an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances. The solutions architect is designing a warm standby DR site in us-west-2. The business requires that the secondary region can handle 50% of peak traffic immediately during a failover without scaling lag, while minimizing steady-state costs. How should the architect configure the compute layer in us-west-2?

options.text: Deploy AWS Lambda functions in us-west-2 behind an API Gateway to handle failover traffic dynamically without maintaining any running EC2 instances.
Maintain an identical Auto Scaling group in us-west-2 configured with the exact same minimum and maximum instance counts as us-east-1.
Set the minimum capacity of the us-west-2 Auto Scaling group to zero instances, relying on launch templates and instance provisioning speed during an emergency.
Configure an Auto Scaling group in us-west-2 with a minimum capacity that supports 50% of peak traffic, scaling up as demand dictates.

questions.explanation: A warm standby disaster recovery strategy involves keeping a scaled-down version of a fully functional stack running in a secondary region. Configuring the Auto Scaling group minimum capacity to meet the immediate percentage requirement balances instant availability upon failover with optimized cost.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Rewriting the architecture to serverless compute for DR introduces significant engineering effort and behavioral discrepancies from the primary EC2-based application.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Running identical instance counts in the secondary region defeats the cost-saving purpose of a warm standby architecture, leading to unnecessary double capacity costs during normal operations.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Setting minimum capacity to zero creates a pilot light or backup-and-restore model rather than a warm standby, causing severe scaling delays and violating the requirement to handle 50% of traffic immediately.

questions.question: A financial services organization is implementing a multi-region active-active database layer using Amazon DynamoDB Global Tables. The application is deployed in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Users frequently write updates to their profiles from both regions. The compliance team mandates that if a concurrent write occurs on the same record in both regions within milliseconds, no update is silently lost due to arbitrary overwrite. Which feature should the architect enable?

options.text: Enable DynamoDB Streams with AWS Lambda to reconcile conflicting writes asynchronously across regions.
Configure DynamoDB Global Tables with Last-Write-Wins (LWW) timestamp tracking based on client-provided timestamps.
Implement cross-region strong consistency locking via Amazon ElastiCache Global Datastores before writing to DynamoDB.
Use DynamoDB Global Tables with native conflict resolution, ensuring the application handles conditional writes or conflict detection logic since DynamoDB uses last-writer-wins by default.

questions.explanation: Amazon DynamoDB Global Tables provide multi-region replication. By default, they resolve concurrent updates using a last-writer-wins algorithm based on internal timestamps. Architects must design application layers with conditional writes or optimistic concurrency control if strict conflict management is required beyond default behavior.

wrongOptionNotes.A: While streams and Lambda can handle custom conflict resolution, it is complex, asynchronous, and does not leverage the native conflict resolution built into Global Tables.
wrongOptionNotes.B: DynamoDB Global Tables use a default last writer wins model based on physical wall-clock time of the AWS region, but relying on uncoordinated client clocks or simple LWW can result in data loss due to clock drift.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Adding an external caching layer to handle distributed locks across regions introduces network latency and brittle dependency chains, defeating the benefits of DynamoDB Global Tables.

questions.question: An e-commerce platform hosts its static frontend assets in Amazon S3 in us-east-1 and distributes them globally via Amazon CloudFront. The company requires a cross-region disaster recovery strategy for the S3 bucket. If us-east-1 experiences a major outage, the application must failover to a replica bucket in eu-west-1 with minimal manual intervention. How should the architect configure S3 replication?

options.text: Set up a nightly AWS Backup plan to replicate S3 snapshots from us-east-1 to eu-west-1.
Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) from us-east-1 to eu-west-1, and update CloudFront origin failover groups to point to the eu-west-1 bucket as the secondary origin.
Configure S3 Batch Replication from us-east-1 to eu-west-1 and use Route 53 latency-based routing to switch DNS records during an outage.
Deploy a duplicate S3 bucket in eu-west-1 and modify client-side application code to upload files to both buckets simultaneously.

questions.explanation: Amazon S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) replicates objects across AWS Regions automatically. When paired with Amazon CloudFront origin failover, CloudFront can automatically failover to the secondary S3 origin when the primary origin experiences HTTP 5xx errors, ensuring high availability and seamless DR.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Backups taken nightly introduce a 24-hour RPO, which is inadequate for real-time web asset disaster recovery.
wrongOptionNotes.C: S3 Batch Replication is designed for replicating existing historical objects, not continuous real-time replication of incoming dynamic uploads.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Dual client-side uploads increase client bandwidth usage, application complexity, and introduce consistency risks if one upload fails.

questions.question: A media corporation is designing a disaster recovery solution for its core asset-ingestion pipeline. The primary region is us-east-1, and the backup region is us-west-2. The RPO is 0 hours (no data loss for committed objects), and the RTO is 4 hours. The pipeline relies on Amazon S3 buckets. Which configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Schedule an AWS Lambda function running every 6 hours to sync new files between the primary and backup S3 buckets using the AWS CLI.
Enable Amazon S3 Versioning without replication, and manually copy objects during a disaster event.
Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) with S3 Replication Time Control (RTC) enabled between us-east-1 and us-west-2.
Use AWS Storage Gateway cached volumes in us-east-1 with daily snapshots exported to us-west-2.

questions.explanation: Amazon S3 Cross-Region Replication with S3 Replication Time Control (RTC) is engineered to replicate 99.99% of new objects within 15 minutes, making it the ideal service to achieve an RPO of 0 (or near-zero) for S3 buckets in multi-region DR architectures.

wrongOptionNotes.A: A 6-hour scheduled sync results in an RPO of at least 6 hours, failing the zero data loss requirement.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Manual copying during an emergency introduces human error and makes meeting a 4-hour RTO difficult for large datasets.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Daily snapshots provide a 24-hour RPO, failing the zero data loss requirement.

questions.question: An enterprise runs an active-passive multi-region web application where us-east-1 is primary and us-west-2 is secondary. Amazon Route 53 is used for DNS routing with health checks. During a disaster simulation, the us-east-1 region's web servers were shut down, but Route 53 did not immediately failover traffic to us-west-2. What is the most likely cause of this delay?

options.text: Amazon S3 replication lag prevented the web servers in us-west-2 from starting up.
AWS Shield Advanced blocked the failover traffic as a suspected volumetric DDoS attack.
The Time to Live (TTL) on the Route 53 DNS record was set to a high value, causing local DNS resolvers and client browsers to continue caching the primary region IP address.
Route 53 health checks require manual confirmation from an administrator before triggering a failover.

questions.explanation: DNS failover speed is heavily dependent on the Time to Live (TTL) value configured on the DNS records. Lower TTLs (e.g., 60 seconds) allow clients and recursive resolvers to discover updated routing records much faster during an outage.

wrongOptionNotes.A: S3 replication has no bearing on DNS resolution or Route 53 health check evaluations.
wrongOptionNotes.B: AWS Shield does not block legitimate failover traffic or interfere with Route 53 health check routing logic.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Route 53 health checks operate automatically without requiring manual administrator intervention.

questions.question: A retail company is building a disaster recovery architecture for its core inventory database running on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL in us-east-1. The DR requirement is to maintain a replica in us-west-2 with an RPO of under 5 minutes and an RTO of under 15 minutes. Cost optimization is a key priority. Which approach should the architect take?

options.text: Deploy a cross-region Amazon RDS Read Replica in us-west-2, and configure application orchestration scripts to promote the replica to a standalone primary database upon primary failure.
Deploy a fully provisioned Multi-AZ RDS instance with active multi-region replication enabled directly via RDS settings in us-west-2.
Use AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) with full load and ongoing replication to sync to an Amazon DynamoDB table in us-west-2.
Take daily snapshots of the RDS database in us-east-1 and copy them to us-west-2 using automated backup plans.

questions.explanation: An Amazon RDS cross-region read replica provides an asynchronous replica in a secondary region at minimal cost. It meets strict RPO/RTO targets when paired with promotion scripts, avoiding the high cost of running a fully-provisioned active-active database instance.

wrongOptionNotes.B: RDS does not support synchronous multi-region active-active clusters natively without using Aurora Global Databases, and running a fully provisioned primary instance in a second region violates cost optimization goals.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Migrating a relational PostgreSQL schema to DynamoDB introduces significant application refactoring and does not satisfy relational database DR constraints cost-effectively.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Daily snapshots result in an RPO of up to 24 hours, failing the requirement of an RPO under 5 minutes.

questions.question: A financial company operates a microservices architecture on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate in us-east-1. To comply with business continuity mandates, the company needs a disaster recovery setup in us-west-2. The RTO must be less than 5 minutes, and the RPO must be near zero. The database is already replicated using Aurora Global Databases. How should the architect configure the ECS compute layer in us-west-2?

options.text: Maintain an identical active ECS service deployment in us-west-2 running the same task count as us-east-1, fronted by global load balancing.
Migrate all container workloads to AWS Lambda in us-east-1 and remove the us-west-2 disaster recovery requirement.
Rely entirely on AWS CloudFormation templates stored in us-west-2 to deploy the ECS cluster and services only after an outage is declared.
Keep ECS services running in us-west-2 at zero task count, relying on automated scaling groups to launch tasks when triggered.

questions.explanation: For strict RTOs under 5 minutes on container platforms like Amazon ECS with Fargate, maintaining running task instances in the secondary region ensures zero provisioning delay during failover events.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Serverless migration does not satisfy multi-region disaster recovery mandates.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Deploying an entire container infrastructure via CloudFormation during an outage takes significant time, easily exceeding a 5-minute RTO.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Fargate does not use Auto Scaling groups of EC2 instances; while Fargate service scaling can be triggered, starting tasks from zero count can introduce container provisioning delays that risk exceeding a 5-minute RTO.

questions.question: A digital media platform stores high-value video master files in Amazon S3 in us-east-1. The company requires a backup copy in eu-west-1. Regulatory compliance dictates that all replicated objects must be locked using S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode to prevent accidental or malicious deletion for 5 years. How should the solutions architect configure this?

options.text: Use an AWS Lambda function triggered by S3 event notifications to copy files to eu-west-1 and apply bucket policies.
Enable S3 Object Lock on both the source and replica buckets, and configure S3 Cross-Region Replication to copy objects along with their Object Lock retention settings.
Apply IAM deny policies on the destination bucket preventing any user or role from deleting objects.
Enable S3 Object Lock only on the destination bucket in eu-west-1 and rely on standard S3 CRR to transfer files.

questions.explanation: Amazon S3 Cross-Region Replication integrates natively with S3 Object Lock. By enabling Object Lock on both buckets, retention settings and compliance controls are securely replicated across regions.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Custom Lambda replication code is unnecessary and prone to failure or security gaps when native S3 CRR with Object Lock integration is available.
wrongOptionNotes.C: IAM policies can be modified or overridden by administrative credentials, whereas S3 Object Lock Compliance mode prevents even the root user from deleting objects during the retention period.
wrongOptionNotes.D: S3 CRR replication of locked objects requires S3 Object Lock to be enabled on both source and destination buckets with compatible retention modes.

questions.question: A global enterprise runs its primary applications in us-east-1 and maintains a disaster recovery environment in us-west-2. The network team wants to connect both VPCs securely with private IP connectivity that bypasses the public internet, ensuring high bandwidth and consistent network performance. Which AWS service provides the most resilient cross-region connectivity?

options.text: AWS Site-to-Site VPN connections configured between virtual private gateways in both regions.
AWS Transit Gateway with inter-region peering attachments between us-east-1 and us-west-2.
VPC Peering connections established directly between us-east-1 and us-west-2 VPCs.
Direct Connect connections terminating in an on-premises data center, bridging traffic between us-east-1 and us-west-2 via hair-pinning.

questions.explanation: AWS Transit Gateway inter-region peering allows architects to seamlessly connect VPCs and on-premises networks across different AWS Regions over the private AWS global network backbone with high throughput and robust encryption.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Site-to-Site VPN traverses the public internet, introducing potential bandwidth bottlenecks, latency fluctuations, and lower throughput compared to native private backbone connections.
wrongOptionNotes.C: VPC peering does not support cross-region peering across all legacy architectures without Transit Gateway, but more importantly, cross-region VPC peering uses the secure AWS global network; however, AWS Transit Gateway with inter-region peering or native cross-region VPC peering is standard. Wait, cross-region VPC peering is supported, but AWS Transit Gateway inter-region peering provides centralized routing and management for multi-region architectures.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Routing cross-region cloud traffic through an on-premises data center introduces unnecessary latency, egress costs, and a single point of failure.

questions.question: An e-commerce company operates a multi-region workload across us-east-1 and eu-west-1. The frontend web tier runs on Amazon EC2 behind Application Load Balancers. The company uses AWS Global Accelerator to route client traffic globally. A fiber cut disrupts connectivity to us-east-1. How does AWS Global Accelerator handle the failure?

options.text: Global Accelerator requires DNS propagation delay of up to 30 minutes before client traffic is shifted to eu-west-1.
Global Accelerator fails over by switching the underlying Route 53 CNAME record associated with the ALB.
Global Accelerator drops all incoming connections until an administrator manually updates the accelerator endpoint weight table.

Global Accelerator automatically detects the unhealthy endpoint health status via integrated endpoint health checks and reroutes user traffic to the healthy application endpoints in eu-west-1 within seconds.

questions.explanation: AWS Global Accelerator uses static anycast IP addresses that anchor to AWS edge locations worldwide. It routes traffic over the resilient AWS global network and automatically fails over to healthy regional endpoints within seconds when health checks fail.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Global Accelerator uses anycast static IP addresses rather than DNS-based resolution, eliminating DNS caching and propagation delays.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Global Accelerator uses AWS edge locations and static anycast IP addresses, bypassing standard DNS CNAME switching mechanisms.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Global Accelerator performs automatic failover without requiring manual intervention.

questions.question: An architecture team is designing a disaster recovery plan for an enterprise workload on Amazon EC2. The business has a low budget for the DR site (Pilot Light model) but requires that core application state and database transactions are never lost (RPO = 0). The database runs on Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. What is the most cost-effective and compliant architecture for the compute and database tiers?

options.text: Use weekly EBS volume snapshots copied to the DR region and restore instances manually when needed.
Deploy an Aurora Global Database with a secondary read/write instance in the DR region, and keep a full fleet of EC2 instances running 24/7.

Deploy an Aurora Global Database for zero-data-loss replication, and store pre-configured EC2 AMI and CloudFormation templates in the DR region to provision compute instances only when a failover is declared.
Maintain an active-active multi-region Aurora cluster with fully scaled EC2 instances running behind a Network Load Balancer in both regions.

questions.explanation: The Pilot Light model keeps critical data synchronized (e.g., via Aurora Global Databases for RPO=0) while keeping compute infrastructure minimal or unprovisioned until disaster recovery is triggered, optimizing costs.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Weekly EBS snapshots result in an unacceptable RPO of up to 7 days for a mission-critical workload.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Keeping a full fleet of EC2 instances running 24/7 in the DR region contradicts the Pilot Light cost-saving model.
wrongOptionNotes.D: An active-active fully provisioned multi-region setup is expensive and violates the low-budget Pilot Light requirement.

questions.question: A multinational financial firm is building a disaster recovery strategy for its core analytics platform. Large datasets (hundreds of terabytes) stored in Amazon S3 in us-east-1 must be accessible in eu-west-1 within 2 hours of a disaster declaration. The company wants to minimize storage and data transfer costs while adhering to this RTO. What is the most efficient storage replication strategy?

options.text: Store data exclusively in us-east-1 and execute an AWS Snowball import/export job to move data to eu-west-1 during a disaster.
Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) to continuously replicate all S3 objects from us-east-1 to eu-west-1 in real time.
Keep buckets empty in eu-west-1 and write a Python script to copy data over the internet using AWS CLI during a disaster.
Use Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval for the primary bucket and restore archives to eu-west-1 on demand.

questions.explanation: Continuous replication using Amazon S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) ensures data is present in the disaster recovery region ahead of time, eliminating data transfer delays during an outage and easily meeting tight RTOs for large datasets.

wrongOptionNotes.A: AWS Snowball physical shipping takes days, completely violating a 2-hour RTO.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Copying hundreds of terabytes over the internet during an active disaster introduces massive bottlenecks, potential network throttling, and failure to meet the RTO.
wrongOptionNotes.D: S3 Glacier restoration takes hours to days depending on retrieval tiers, making it unsuitable for a 2-hour RTO requirement.

questions.question: An enterprise application hosted on Amazon EC2 instances in us-east-1 uses Amazon DynamoDB for user session management. The company is implementing a multi-region disaster recovery architecture in us-west-2. Session data must be available globally with low latency and automatic multi-region replication. Which DynamoDB feature should the solutions architect implement?

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB Streams paired with custom AWS Lambda replication scripts
Amazon Aurora Global Databases with a DynamoDB compatibility wrapper
Scheduled Amazon DynamoDB point-in-time recovery (PITR) exports to S3 with cross-region replication
Amazon DynamoDB Global Tables

questions.explanation: Amazon DynamoDB Global Tables leverage multi-region replication to provide fully managed active-active table synchronization across AWS Regions, making them ideal for globally distributed session stores and low-latency disaster recovery.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Custom replication scripts via DynamoDB Streams and Lambda introduce operational complexity and maintenance overhead compared to native Global Tables.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Amazon Aurora is a relational database service and does not provide DynamoDB compatibility wrappers or session store capabilities directly.
wrongOptionNotes.C: PITR and backup exports are designed for historical recovery, not active low-latency multi-region synchronization.

questions.question: A healthcare analytics company runs a high-throughput data processing pipeline using AWS Lambda functions triggered by an Amazon S3 bucket. The Lambda functions read small JSON files, extract metadata, and insert records into an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database. Recently, unpredictable bursts of traffic have caused the Lambda concurrency to skyrocket, exhausting the database connection pool and leading to high error rates and increased costs due to excessive retries. Which architectural pattern should a solutions architect implement to cost-effectively optimize this pipeline?

options.text: Implement Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the database and set Lambda concurrency limits to a very low static number.
Migrate the Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database to a multi-region deployment to distribute the write load across multiple read replicas.
Increase the provisioned memory and CPU of the Lambda functions to speed up execution time and reduce the window of database connection exhaustion.
Place an Amazon SQS FIFO queue between the S3 event notification and the Lambda function, and configure the Lambda event source mapping with a batch size.

questions.explanation: Buffering asynchronous workloads with Amazon SQS is a foundational pattern for decoupling producers from consumers, protecting downstream resources like databases from unpredictable spikes, and optimizing compute costs.

wrongOptionNotes.A: While RDS Proxy helps manage database connections, setting a very low static concurrency limit without a queuing mechanism will lead to dropped events or excessive S3 retry loops.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Read replicas cannot handle write traffic in standard Aurora configurations, and a multi-region deployment adds unnecessary operational complexity and cost for handling spikes.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Scaling up Lambda compute does not solve the fundamental connection pooling issue caused by concurrent spikes; it often increases costs without protecting downstream databases.

questions.question: An enterprise web application runs on Amazon EC2 instances managed by an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. The application experiences predictable diurnal traffic patterns, with heavy load during business hours and very low traffic overnight. Currently, the fleet maintains a static minimum capacity to handle peak hours, leading to unnecessary compute charges during off-peak hours. Which solution provides the most cost-effective architecture while maintaining high availability?

options.text: Implement dynamic scaling policies based on high CPU utilization thresholds combined with a target tracking scaling policy.
Switch all EC2 instances to Dedicated Instances to leverage volume discounts for long-running infrastructure.
Configure Auto Scaling scheduled scaling actions to scale out the capacity before business hours and scale in the capacity during off-peak hours.
Migrate the entire workload to AWS Lambda to eliminate server idle costs entirely without modifying the application codebase.

questions.explanation: When workloads exhibit predictable, cyclical traffic trends, scheduled scaling actions prevent wasteful over-provisioning during low-traffic periods without sacrificing responsiveness.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Dynamic scaling is reactive and can introduce latency when scaling up from a low minimum capacity during sudden traffic surges, whereas scheduled scaling handles known patterns proactively.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Dedicated Instances are more expensive than shared tenancy instances and do not solve the problem of running unneeded capacity during off-peak hours.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Rewriting or containerizing an enterprise application for Lambda is not always feasible and may introduce cold start latency and architectural refactoring costs.

questions.question: A financial technology firm stores 100 TB of compliance audit logs in an Amazon S3 bucket. The compliance policy states that these logs must be immediately accessible for 30 days, accessed infrequently for the next 60 days, and then archived for 7 years where they are rarely accessed but must be retrievable within hours. Retrieval requests during the archive phase must be predictable and cost-effective. Which lifecycle configuration is most cost-efficient?

options.text: Store all objects in Amazon EBS General Purpose SSD (gp3) volumes attached to an archival EC2 instance.
Transition objects directly from S3 Standard to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days.
Transition objects to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 30 days, and then to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 90 days.
Keep all objects in S3 Standard for the entire 7-year duration and utilize S3 Select to filter logs when auditors request them.

questions.explanation: Aligning S3 storage classes with data access patterns using S3 Lifecycle policies ensures cost optimization while respecting minimum storage duration constraints (e.g., 30 days for IA, 90 days for Glacier Flexible Retrieval, 180 days for Deep Archive).

wrongOptionNotes.A: EBS volumes are significantly more expensive than S3 for large-scale object storage and lack built-in lifecycle archiving policies.
wrongOptionNotes.B: S3 Glacier Deep Archive has a 180-day minimum storage charge. Transitioning objects out after only 30 days would trigger early deletion fees, negating cost savings.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Storing 100 TB in S3 Standard for 7 years incurs massive, unnecessary storage costs compared to transitioning colder data to tiered storage classes.

questions.question: An analytics startup runs resource-intensive containerized batch jobs on Amazon ECS with Amazon EC2 launch types. The batch jobs are triggered randomly throughout the day and take between 15 to 45 minutes to complete. The engineering team notices that the EC2 instances remain running and idle for long periods between job executions, resulting in high infrastructure costs. Which architectural change should the solutions architect recommend to optimize costs?

options.text: Configure an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to stop the EC2 instances when CPU utilization drops below 5 percent for 60 minutes.
Migrate the ECS tasks from the EC2 launch type to the AWS Fargate launch type.
Scale down the Auto Scaling group backing the ECS cluster to zero instances when no jobs are running.
Purchase Compute Savings Plans covering all potential peak capacity across the entire cluster.

questions.explanation: For intermittent, unpredictable batch workloads, serverless container options like AWS Fargate eliminate idle server overhead and align compute billing strictly with task execution duration.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Stopping ECS cluster instance nodes arbitrarily via CloudWatch without coordinating with the ECS scheduler can orphan tasks, cause deployment failures, and disrupt the cluster health.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Scaling an ECS EC2-backed cluster down to zero requires complex orchestration with cluster capacity providers and can cause task launch failures if container instances are not available to register tasks.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While Savings Plans offer discounts, they do not eliminate the cost of keeping idle instances running if the underlying architecture still requires EC2 capacity to be provisioned 24/7.

questions.question: A digital media platform caches high-resolution image assets using Amazon CloudFront with an Application Load Balancer origin. Due to frequent cache invalidations requested by content editors, the cache hit ratio has dropped to 40 percent. This has caused a massive surge in origin requests, driving up EC2 and NAT Gateway data transfer costs. Which strategy best mitigates these costs while maintaining cache freshness?

options.text: Increase the Application Load Balancer capacity units to handle the higher volume of cache miss requests.
Deploy a NAT Gateway in every Availability Zone to distribute the data transfer costs evenly across subnets.
Disable CloudFront caching entirely and route all traffic directly through the Application Load Balancer to ensure end users always see the latest images.
Implement CloudFront cache policies using query strings and headers selectively, and use object versioning in the origin URLs instead of frequent cache invalidations.

questions.explanation: Frequent CloudFront invalidations drive up costs and reduce cache efficiency. Utilizing versioned filenames or content hashes allows content updates to propagate efficiently without costly invalidation requests.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Scaling up infrastructure components to absorb inefficient caching is an anti-pattern that increases operational costs instead of fixing the root cause.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Adding more NAT Gateways increases hourly fixed infrastructure costs and does not reduce the volume of data transferred through them.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Bypassing CloudFront increases origin load, degrades latency, and significantly inflates data transfer and compute costs.

questions.question: An enterprise organization runs a large database fleet on Amazon RDS for MySQL. A financial audit reveals that several non-production database instances in development and staging environments are provisioned with multi-AZ deployments and provisioned IOPS (io1) storage, matching production specifications. These instances run only 8 hours a day, 5 days a week. Which combination of actions will yield the highest immediate cost reduction without impacting developer productivity?

options.text: Purchase 3-year All Upfront RDS Reserved Instances for all development and staging database instances.
Convert the instances to Single-AZ deployments, change storage to General Purpose SSD (gp3), and implement AWS Instance Scheduler to stop instances outside business hours.
Enable RDS Performance Insights and set the retention period to 7 days across all development databases.
Migrate the development databases to Amazon DynamoDB using on-demand capacity mode.

questions.explanation: Non-production environments represent prime targets for cost optimization through right-sizing (Single-AZ and gp3 storage) and automated scheduling to ensure resources do not incur charges when idle.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Committing to 3-year Reserved Instances for non-production environments that may change or become obsolete locks in capital for resources that should instead be turned off when not in use.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Enabling Performance Insights adds monitoring capabilities and potential costs, doing nothing to address oversized storage or running hours.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Rewriting MySQL database schemas and application queries for DynamoDB just for cost reduction in dev environments introduces excessive engineering overhead.

questions.question: A global software company hosts a static documentation website in an Amazon S3 bucket fronted by Amazon CloudFront. The website receives steady traffic globally. The security team mandates that all traffic must be encrypted in transit and that unauthorized direct access to the S3 bucket must be blocked. To minimize operational overhead and egress costs, how should the solutions architect configure this setup?

options.text: Configure CloudFront to access the S3 bucket using an Origin Access Control (OAC) and enforce bucket policies denying public access.
Attach an Elastic Load Balancer in front of the S3 bucket and configure SSL termination at the load balancer level.
Make the S3 bucket public and configure bucket ACLs to allow read access exclusively from CloudFront IP address ranges published in AWS JSON files.
Route all user traffic directly to the S3 website endpoint over HTTP and rely on CloudFront for DNS resolution only.

questions.explanation: Using CloudFront Origin Access Control (OAC) secures S3 bucket origins effectively, preventing direct public access while allowing secure content delivery at scale.

wrongOptionNotes.B: S3 natively supports HTTPS and does not require an Elastic Load Balancer, which would introduce unnecessary monthly infrastructure costs and architectural complexity.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Relying on public S3 buckets restricted by changing IP ranges is an anti-pattern that creates security vulnerabilities and maintenance overhead.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Serving traffic over HTTP violates encryption-in-transit mandates, and bypassing CloudFront edge caching increases data transfer costs and latency.

questions.question: An analytics enterprise stores 300 TB of research data in Amazon S3. The data is accessed unpredictably: some objects are read multiple times a day, while others are not accessed for months. The company wants to minimize storage costs without incurring retrieval fees or experiencing latency penalties when accessing frequently used files. Which S3 storage tier is the most cost-effective choice?

options.text: Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
Amazon S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA)
Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering
Amazon S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access

questions.explanation: S3 Intelligent-Tiering is designed for data with unknown or changing access patterns, automatically optimizing costs across access tiers without retrieval fees.

wrongOptionNotes.A: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval introduces retrieval delays ranging from minutes to hours, making it unsuitable for data that needs to be accessed immediately.
wrongOptionNotes.B: S3 Standard-IA charges retrieval fees per gigabyte, which makes it cost-prohibitive and unpredictable for data with mixed access patterns that include frequent reads.
wrongOptionNotes.D: S3 One Zone-IA stores data in a single Availability Zone, risking data loss during an AZ outage, and still incurs retrieval fees for data access.

questions.question: A financial firm runs a mission-critical message processing application on Amazon EC2 instances across three Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. The workload is steady and continuous 24/7. Currently, the instances are running on On-Demand pricing. The finance department requires a cost optimization plan that guarantees capacity availability in the event of an AZ failure while maximizing financial savings over a 1-year commitment. Which pricing model should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Purchase Amazon EC2 Standard Reserved Instances tied to specific instance types in a single Availability Zone.
Migrate all EC2 instances to Spot Instances backed by an Auto Scaling group with diversification strategies.
Rely entirely on On-Demand capacity reservation blocks purchased for 3 years.
Purchase Compute Savings Plans with a 1-year term covering the baseline vCPU and memory usage across the fleet.

questions.explanation: Compute Savings Plans offer the best balance of flexibility, high discount rates, and regional resilience for steady, 24/7 enterprise workloads running on Amazon EC2.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Standard RIs tied to a single Availability Zone can create capacity constraints or failure risks if an AZ goes down and instances need to be launched elsewhere.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Spot Instances can be interrupted with a two-minute warning, which is unacceptable for a mission-critical message processing workload requiring high availability.
wrongOptionNotes.C: On-Demand Capacity Reservations guarantee capacity but do not offer the significant billing discounts associated with Savings Plans.

questions.question: An e-commerce company operates a containerized microservices application on Amazon EKS. The cluster runs on a mix of On-Demand and Spot EC2 instances managed by Karpenter. During flash sales, traffic spikes rapidly, but new pods occasionally remain in a Pending state because the cluster takes several minutes to provision new EC2 nodes. To balance performance and cost efficiency, what is the best approach to eliminate this provisioning lag?

options.text: Disable Spot instances entirely and rely exclusively on fixed-size EC2 Auto Scaling groups with classic EC2 scaling policies.
Configure Karpenter provisioners with a lightweight warm pool of on-demand capacity or utilize interruption-resistant spot fallback policies with pre-warmed instance node templates.
Migrate all microservices to AWS Lambda and configure provisioned concurrency for every service.
Over-provision the EKS cluster with 300 percent more static On-Demand EC2 instances than peak historical traffic requires.

questions.explanation: Karpenter optimizes EKS node provisioning speed and cost, but combining it with intelligent node structuring or minimal warm capacity prevents scaling latency during sudden flash sales.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Removing Spot instances eliminates significant cost savings, and traditional ASGs are slower and less granular than Karpenter for EKS workloads.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Using provisioned concurrency across all microservices at scale can become exceedingly expensive and requires extensive refactoring of long-running containerized code.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Over-provisioning massive static capacity defeats the cost-optimization purpose of using dynamic autoscalers like Karpenter and Spot instances.

questions.question: A retail corporation runs a centralized data lake on Amazon S3. Multiple business units upload CSV and Parquet files into a single landing bucket. A weekly Apache Spark job running on Amazon EMR reads the entire dataset to generate executive reports. Over the years, billions of tiny files (less than 10 KB each) have accumulated in the bucket. The EMR job execution time has increased threefold, and S3 API request costs have surged. Which action resolves this performance and cost degradation?

options.text: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering on the bucket to automatically compress files in the archive tier.
Implement a routine compaction job using AWS Glue or Spark to merge small files into larger, optimized objects (e.g., 128 MB to 512 MB).
Migrate all data from Amazon S3 to Amazon EBS provisioned IOPS (io2) volumes attached to the EMR master node.
Upgrade the Amazon EMR cluster instance types to memory-optimized instances with higher network bandwidth.

questions.explanation: Addressing the 'small file problem' via compaction is essential for optimizing S3 request costs and analytics query performance on distributed processing engines like EMR.

wrongOptionNotes.A: S3 Intelligent-Tiering does not combine or compact discrete objects; it only moves individual objects between storage tiers based on access.
wrongOptionNotes.C: EBS volumes cannot be easily shared across distributed EMR nodes as a native data lake store, and costs would be astronomically high for hundreds of terabytes of data.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Upgrading hardware does not solve the root cause of S3 API throttling and overhead caused by billions of tiny file listings and metadata requests.

questions.question: An online education platform stores video lecture recordings in an Amazon S3 bucket. Students stream these videos globally. The company notices that data transfer out (DTO) charges from Amazon S3 to the internet are accounting for 60 percent of their monthly AWS bill. Which architectural pattern will reduce these data transfer costs while improving video playback performance?

options.text: Deploy NAT Gateways in every Availability Zone to route student video requests through private IP addresses.
Front the S3 bucket with Amazon CloudFront and utilize CloudFront origin access control (OAC) to cache video segments at edge locations globally.
Replicate the S3 bucket across every AWS region globally using S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR).
Attach Elastic IP addresses to the S3 bucket to bypass standard internet routing fees.

questions.explanation: Caching static and media assets via Amazon CloudFront dramatically reduces direct S3-to-internet egress costs by leveraging AWS's global edge network and lower data transfer pricing tiers.

wrongOptionNotes.A: NAT Gateways are used for outbound traffic from private subnets to the internet, not for serving public content from S3 to global users, and would add heavy hourly and data processing charges.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Cross-Region Replication incurs massive storage and replication data transfer costs across all regions without solving the cost of egress from S3 to end users.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Elastic IP addresses cannot be attached directly to Amazon S3 buckets; they are reserved for Amazon EC2 instances and NAT gateways.

questions.question: A financial services firm runs a batch processing workload on Amazon EC2 instances managed by an Auto Scaling group. The jobs execute every weekend, taking exactly 10 hours to complete. Currently, the company uses On-Demand instances, resulting in high costs. The engineering team wants to optimize costs while ensuring that instances are not terminated mid-job. What is the most cost-effective deployment strategy?

options.text: Migrate the batch jobs to AWS Lambda with a maximum timeout configured to 15 minutes.
Use Amazon EC2 Spot Instances with an instance diversification strategy across multiple instance types and Availability Zones, combined with Spot Instance interruption notices handled gracefully.
Purchase 3-year EC2 Standard Reserved Instances covering the weekend batch capacity.
Purchase Dedicated Hosts to ensure isolation and compliance during weekend processing windows.

questions.explanation: Spot Instances provide maximum cost reduction for fault-tolerant or restartable batch workloads, provided the architecture incorporates instance pool diversification.

wrongOptionNotes.A: AWS Lambda has a hard maximum timeout of 15 minutes, making it impossible to run batch jobs that take 10 hours without complete re-architecting into micro-tasks.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Purchasing 3-year RIs for instances that run only 10 hours a week results in low utilization efficiency, making it far more expensive than Spot instances or On-Demand when used selectively.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Dedicated Hosts are the most expensive EC2 tenancy option, intended for strict licensing requirements, and do not make sense for cost-optimized batch processing.

questions.question: An enterprise company operates a multi-tier web application running on Amazon EC2 instances. The database tier runs on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. The database is heavily over-provisioned with db.r6g.4xlarge instances because of sporadic traffic peaks during end-of-month reporting. The finance team mandates that the database infrastructure costs must be reduced without risking database stability. What is the most architectural-sound recommendation?

options.text: Convert the RDS instance to a General Purpose SSD (gp2) storage type with minimal allocated storage.
Enable Multi-AZ standby instances in two additional AWS regions to split the reporting read traffic.
Implement Amazon ElastiCache for Redis in front of the database to cache frequent read queries, and right-size the RDS instance to a smaller size.
Scale the RDS instance vertically to db.r6g.8xlarge to ensure reporting queries execute faster during peak windows.

questions.explanation: Caching query results with Amazon ElastiCache offloads repetitive compute and memory tasks from relational databases, enabling significant cost savings through effective database right-sizing.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Storage type changes alone do not relieve CPU and memory pressure caused by unoptimized or heavy query loads during reporting peaks.
wrongOptionNotes.B: RDS Multi-AZ standby instances are for high availability and failover, not for serving read traffic, and cross-region architectures add substantial cost and replication latency.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Scaling up increases infrastructure costs further, directly violating the mandate to reduce database expenses.

questions.question: A digital marketing agency hosts client websites on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The architecture includes AWS WAF (Web Application Firewall) attached to the ALB to inspect incoming web requests. The finance department reviews the AWS bill and discovers that AWS WAF web ACL inspection fees and request body inspection charges are exceptionally high, exceeding the cost of the EC2 instances themselves. How can the solutions architect optimize WAF costs without compromising application security?

options.text: Remove AWS WAF entirely and rely solely on security groups attached to the EC2 instances.
Purchase an AWS WAF Reserved Capacity plan for a 3-year term.
Review WAF rule statements, scope down rule inspection criteria to exclude static asset paths, and disable unnecessary inspection of request bodies for trusted endpoints.
Migrate the web applications from Amazon EC2 to Amazon S3 static website hosting.

questions.explanation: Optimizing AWS WAF costs requires auditing rule definitions, limiting inspection scope to sensitive paths (e.g., login or API endpoints), and avoiding deep payload inspection on static resources.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Security groups only operate at the IP and port level; removing WAF leaves the web application vulnerable to Layer 7 attacks like SQL injection and cross-site scripting.
wrongOptionNotes.B: AWS WAF does not offer reserved capacity pricing models; billing is strictly pay-per-use based on rules and request volumes.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Client websites running dynamic application code cannot be hosted purely as static S3 websites without breaking backend functionality.

questions.question: A global gaming company runs its user authentication microservice on Amazon ECS with the Fargate launch type, fronted by an Application Load Balancer. Following a sudden surge in player logins, users experience intermittent 504 Gateway Timeouts. Inspection of the ECS service metrics shows that container CPU utilization is at 100% and tasks are repeatedly being terminated and replaced due to failed health checks during initialization. What is the most cost-effective architectural remediation to resolve the timeouts and stabilize the service?

options.text: Provision a multi-AZ Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 database to offload user session state and eliminate lock contention during peak login hours.
Migrate the ECS tasks from Fargate to Amazon EC2 launch type using c5.2xlarge instances to ensure dedicated hardware performance without resource contention.
Deploy an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the Application Load Balancer to cache authentication responses and reduce the direct load on the ECS cluster.
Increase the CPU and memory allocation in the ECS task definition, configure target tracking scaling for CPU utilization, and increase the ALB health check timeout and interval parameters.

questions.explanation: When containerized microservices face CPU starvation during startup, health checks often fail because the application cannot respond within the default thresholds, leading to an infinite crash-loop. Right-sizing the task definition and configuring appropriate autoscaling resolves the underlying compute bottleneck.

wrongOptionNotes.A: The bottleneck is container CPU exhaustion during task initialization, not database locking or query performance.
wrongOptionNotes.B: While EC2 provides instance-level control, it introduces infrastructure management overhead and does not inherently solve task sizing or health check tuning issues as cost-effectively as Fargate right-sizing.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Authentication requests are dynamic and unique per user session, making edge caching via CloudFront ineffective for bypassing backend compute limits.

questions.question: A logistics enterprise operates an internal document ingestion workflow using an Amazon S3 bucket that triggers an AWS Lambda function to parse uploaded PDF manifests. Users report that during peak morning hours, a significant percentage of uploads result in 500 errors, and the Lambda function execution logs show frequent throttling exceptions (Rate Exceeded). What architectural adjustment should the solutions architect implement to cost-effectively resolve this pipeline failure?

options.text: Provision dedicated provisioned concurrency for the Lambda function to maintain warm execution environments capable of handling peak arrival rates instantly.
Place an Amazon SQS standard queue between the S3 event notification and the Lambda function, and configure the Lambda event source mapping with appropriate batch sizes and concurrency limits.
Upgrade the Amazon S3 bucket to use requester pays mode so that client applications bear the data transfer costs of handling massive concurrent uploads.
Migrate the processing logic from AWS Lambda to an always-on Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group running behind a Network Load Balancer.

questions.explanation: Direct synchronous triggers from Amazon S3 to AWS Lambda can exhaust account-level concurrent execution limits during spikes. Decoupling the architecture with an Amazon SQS buffer absorbs the load spikes, enables retries, and protects the downstream Lambda function.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Provisioned concurrency helps with cold starts but does not protect against concurrent execution limit exhaustion during extreme traffic bursts, making a queue a more resilient architectural pattern.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Requester pays does not mitigate Lambda concurrency limits or execution throttling issues.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Moving to always-on EC2 instances increases operational cost and complexity, eliminating the serverless benefits when an asynchronous queue can easily solve the throttling issue.

questions.question: An insurance enterprise runs its core customer portal on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer, backed by an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database. During month-end closing, users experience severe latency, and database CPU utilization hits 100% due to complex analytical reporting queries running concurrently with transactional traffic. What design pattern provides the most cost-effective solution without rearchitecting the application code?

options.text: Implement Amazon ElastiCache for Redis in front of the database to cache all SQL query result sets with a 24-hour Time-To-Live.
Create an Amazon RDS Read Replica for the PostgreSQL database and configure the reporting service connection strings to route read-only analytical queries exclusively to the replica.
Scale up the primary RDS instance class to the largest available memory-optimized instance size and enable multi-AZ deployments.
Migrate the primary RDS PostgreSQL database to Amazon DynamoDB to achieve infinitely scalable key-value storage with single-digit millisecond latency.

questions.explanation: Separating read-heavy reporting traffic from transactional traffic using an RDS Read Replica is the standard, most cost-effective architectural pattern for scaling relational database read capacity.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Month-end reporting involves dynamic, non-repeatable aggregations where caching entire result sets with long TTLs is ineffective and risks returning stale financial data.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Scaling up is expensive, does not solve architectural contention between conflicting query types, and hits hardware limits eventually.
